questions.question: Daptomycin.

parts.text: Class of abx?
What is the mechanism of action.
2 organ systems that it can't be used for and why.

questions.model_answer:
a) Class: cyclic lipopeptide.
b) Mechanism of action: daptomycin inserts into the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane in a calcium-dependent manner, causing membrane depolarization and efflux of potassium ions, which halts DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis and leads to rapid, concentration-dependent bacterial cell death (bactericidal), without lysing the cell.
c) 2 organ systems/conditions where it cannot be used and why: (1) Lungs/pneumonia - daptomycin is inactivated/bound by pulmonary surfactant, resulting in inadequate lung tissue activity, so it should not be used to treat pneumonia; (2) CNS infections (meningitis) - daptomycin has poor penetration across the blood-brain barrier/into CSF, making it an unreliable choice for CNS infections.

parts.text: What is the MOA and class of daptomycin?

cohort_answer.text: Lipopeptide: binds to the components of cell membrane rapid depolarization inhibiting intracellular synthesis of DNA/ RNA. Bactericidal in concentration dependent manner. Contraindicated in pneumonia, aside from embolic disease secondary to right-sided endocarditis

parts.text: Why contraindicated in pulmonary infection?
Name class to which it belongs.
Name 2 serious adverse reactions.

cohort_answer.text: Pulmonary contraindication: antimicrobial activity abolished by interaction with pulmonary surfactant; also poor penetration to CNS, bone. Class: Lipopeptides (peak-MIC ratio, 24-hr AUC/MIC, post-antibiotic effect; dose 4-6mg/kg SSTI, 8-10mg/kg severe infections). Adverse reactions: Skeletal muscle toxicity (dose dependent, reversible - D/C if CK>1000 with symptoms or CK>2000 asymptomatic); Eosinophilic pneumonia (usually after 10 days therapy); also severe autoimmune thrombocytopenia/neutropenia, CDI, peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, falsely elevated PT

parts.text: What antimicrobial class does daptomycin belong to?
What is its mechanism of action?
What two organ systems should IV daptomycin NOT be used to treat infections? Give the rationale for each.

cohort_answer.text: Class: lipopeptide. MOA: binds to cell membrane components, causes rapid depolarization; aggregation of daptomycin creates holes that leak ions out of the cell, causing cell death. Not used for: respiratory infections/pneumonia (inhibited by surfactant); CNS infections (does not cross blood-brain barrier, especially with non-inflamed meninges); also prostate.

parts.text: a) Why does it not work for MRSA pneumonia?
b) What class of drug is this?
c) What is the mechanism of action?

cohort_answer.text: a) Inactivated by pulmonary surfactant. b) Lipopeptide. c) Exact mechanism not fully understood; targets cell membrane, binds Ca-dependently by inserting lipophilic tail; causes rapid depolarization via potassium efflux, disrupting DNA/RNA/protein synthesis; bactericidal with minimal cell lysis in S. aureus, less cytokine release.

cohort_answer.text: Daptomycin is not active in the lung (inactivated by pulmonary surfactant).

questions.question: Name the most likely mechanism of resistance

parts.text: Serratia marcescens resistant to ertapenem, imipenem AND meropenem, but susceptible to Ceftriaxone
Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to Meropenem, but susceptible to Imipenem
Staphylococcus aureus resistant to daptomycin
Enterococcus gallinarum resistant to vancomycin, but susceptible to teicoplanin
Enterobacter cloacae intermediate to ertapenem, but susceptible to meropenem and cefepime

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). Pseudomonas: RND efflux pump MexAB-OprM (meropenem/doripenem, but not imipenem, are substrates of this efflux system). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. Enterobacter cloacae: Hyperexpression of ampC + porin change combination.

parts.text: A) Give 2 similarities in pharmacokinetic and spectrum
B) Give 2 differences in the same things

cohort_answer.text: A) Only PK similarity: renal excretion (30% linezolid, ~80% daptomycin). Spectrum: gram positive coverage incl MRSA, VRE. B) Protein binding: Dapto 90% vs Linezolid 31%. CNS penetration: Dapto poor vs Linezolid adequate. Pneumonia: Dapto poor vs Linezolid adequate. Spectrum: Dapto GP only, no mycobacteria vs Linezolid broad GP coverage, mycobacteria covered. Practicality: Dapto IV only, wt based, renal dosing vs Linezolid PO/IV, fixed dose, no renal dosing, high bioavailability.

questions.question: Q41 (2014). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Pt with MRSA pneumonia (Septra R, Macrolides R), switched from vancomycin to daptomycin. Begins to get worse.

parts.text: a) Reason for treatment failure
b) 2 other drugs that could be used, if sensitive

cohort_answer.text: a) Daptomycin antimicrobial activity inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, resulting in failure to reduce bacterial burden in bronchoalveolar pneumonia. b) Linezolid (ZEPHyR study showed superior to vancomycin in MRSA HAP); Telavancin; Ceftaroline; Ceftobiprole; Doxycycline.
